s2.p1: No WDSF member federation. But the island rhythms **ússua** and **socopé** were shaped by ==Portuguese ballroom== dancing.
s2.p2: Every dry-season weekend, villages gather at **fundões**: open-air spaces cordoned off for dancing to local bands.

s3.p: perform each Tchiloli, in troupes known locally as **“tragedies”**. Roles often pass **from father to son**, and men play the female parts.

s4.p1: Fradique and António Mendes Ferreira grew up in **Ribeira Peixe**, in the south of São Tomé. Their sound: **kizomba-pop** and Afropop.
s4.p2: In June 2025 they drew about ==60,000 fans== to Benfica’s **Estádio da Luz** in Lisbon, in a near sell-out.

s5.name: PUÍTA
s5.p: Brought by **Angolan workers**, it became one of the most popular dances on the colonial plantations. After independence, a **national genre**.

s5.name: SOCOPÉ
s5.p: Its name is said to mean **“only with feet”**. Bands played it on outdoor terraces and dance floors, where people came **in crowds** to dance.

s6.p: Colonial authorities **banned the Danço-Congo**, claiming its fast rhythm exhausted dancers and cut their work output. It is often staged on **Independence Day**.

s7.p: The country’s **first** UNESCO intangible heritage: open-air theatre, music and dance in which the emperor’s son is **tried and convicted**.
s7.p2: Africanews reports Tchiloli still **thrives**. One actor plans to teach his oldest child the role of **Kata**, the boy who brings a letter.
